Initially, application replacement was treated as a small startup handoff: the component factory obtained the target object, and the original application callback chain continued to execute. This explained why the object was replaced, but did not establish whether the replacement object already had usable context before it first entered the callback.

Two orderings were on the table.

- Let the replacement object enter the application callback first, then add the outer context.
- Give the replacement object the context required by the callback first, then allow the callback to continue.

The first involved fewer changes. The component factory would not need to take on more object-relationship handling, and the original startup chain would be easier to keep intact. The second was more cautious, but first required an explanation of who establishes the outer object relationship of ContextImpl. There was not enough verification at the time to conclude that either ordering was correct solely because the application could start.

Another easy-to-miss point in the record: replacement completion, the first callback, and the end of the dispatch-phase state are not the same thing. Early discussions focused only on whether onCreate was entered, treating the callback marker as a one-time hint that would naturally be overwritten by subsequent state. This interpretation has not been verified, so do not write it as an implementation requirement yet.

The issue with the DEBUG adapter layer was also left open in the same round. The existing diagnostic text is organized around one call at a time; if multiple threads pass through the same formatting path at nearly the same time, there was no answer as to whether readers could distinguish the sources in the text. Whether thread-related information should be included in the formatted output remains undecided, and the fact that logging is off by default must not change as a result.

The old troubleshooting notes traced the issue name and call name to `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/third_party/lss/linux_syscall_support.h`. That path can serve as an entry point for reviewing local declarations, but it cannot establish that the application-replacement logic belongs in the native support header.

Tentative decision: do not use "startup succeeded" as a substitute for judging the ordering. The next review must examine the context first visible to the replacement object, the first application callback, and the point at which the callback marker exits together; for diagnostic formatting, retain only the possibility that concurrent output may be misread.

# Decision Record for Replacement Callbacks and Thread Diagnostics

Early notes reduced the discussion to "attach first or callback first." After review, this framing is still useful, but it omitted the object handoff itself: the replacement object is not an ordinary newly created Application. It goes through the component factory, name conversion, and the handoff involving the original application objects. Comparing only where a particular call occurs makes it easy to mistake "the object has been replaced" and "the object can already use context in the callback" for the same state.

## Original Conservative Direction

Initially, we leaned toward continuing to use the old callback chain. Once the component factory completed the handoff of the target object, the application lifecycle would proceed first; if the outer object relationship later proved incorrect, the handoff path would fill it in. The reason was not complicated: the startup path already had many adjacent operations, and incorporating the outer-object handling of ContextImpl into the component factory too early would expand the responsibility boundary all at once.

This judgment is retained for now. It explains why the old notes always checked object state after the callback, and why some people then thought that "looking correct in the end" was sufficient. That approach can indeed reduce short-term changes, but it depended on two assumptions that were not written into the interface: the callback would not read application context; the replacement object would not retain the context it saw at that time as subsequent state.

These two assumptions can no longer be treated as default premises. Once the callback reads context, or selects a subsequent branch based on outer context, an after-the-fact fix can only change the later appearance of the object; it cannot undo a branch that has already been taken.

## States Separated During Review

The review did not identify an anomaly that could be uniformly attributed to native calls. The discussion instead returned to the earlier boundary: when the replacement object first enters the application lifecycle, what exactly can it see?

Therefore, the thing previously referred to broadly as "replacement succeeded" is recorded as separate states.

1. The target Application has already been created through the replacement path and has become the handoff object.
2. The object already has the context relationship required by this callback.
3. The callback has finished dispatching, and the state from the dispatch period can be settled.

An uninterrupted startup can only indicate that the first item most likely occurred; it cannot serve as evidence for the second. The second requires checking whether the object relationship is stable when the callback begins; the third requires separately checking whether callback flag is still present. Once these are separated, the original debate is no longer simply "which line comes first," but when each state should hold.

The review rejected only the claim that "adding it after the callback is equivalent." At the time, the final ownership of the component factory and ContextImpl had not been assigned. Unsafe sequencing and implementation ownership still being open for discussion are two different matters.

## Old Handling Method Retained

The recommendation in the old notes was as follows; it is retained here to explain why the position later changed: first execute the replacement object's application callback; if context is later found to be inconsistent, correct outer context; callback flag can wait for the next state update to overwrite it.

It is no longer treated as the default handling. The issue is not that it causes an anomaly every time, but that failure depends on whether the callback reads the object relationship. Objects that do not read the relationship may be completely unaffected; objects that have already read it cannot be returned to the decision point before the callback through an after-the-fact fix.

The callback flag handling is also not rigorous enough. It describes the current dispatch window and should not rely on the next startup, the next callback, or another object action to complete the previous cleanup. Exceptional dispatch in particular cannot entrust cleanup to a future normal path.

## Limits of Path Clues

Earlier troubleshooting looked for hook traces near `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/third_party/lss/linux_syscall_support.h`, then tried to infer the timing of application replacement. This file can still help verify local declarations in the old notes, but there is no evidence that the application callback order is defined here.

This does not mean that proximity to native code is entirely irrelevant, but proximity in a path cannot be used to infer proximity of responsibility. When continuing along this clue, it should be treated as historical navigation rather than treating the syscall wrapper layer as the decision point for application lifecycle timing.

## Addendum on Diagnostic Text

thread-aware diagnostic formatting was initially regarded as a very small debugging change: add some thread-related information to the DEBUG text so that the investigation would involve fewer guesses about its source. The review found that it was not merely a formatting issue. During temporary single-thread debugging, a line of text is usually enough to correspond to one call; when multiple threads pass through the same adapter layer at nearby times, text with identical or nearly identical content may be misread as the same call chain.

At the time, there were two options.

- Keep the old format and rely on external trace to distinguish threads when output is concurrent.
- Retain thread-related context in the formatting adapter layer so that a single diagnostic text entry can distinguish its source.

The first works when trace is complete, but is not suitable as a long-term dependency. Diagnostic text may be excerpted, transferred, stored, or forwarded separately, and external correlation may no longer be available then. The second does not mean writing all internal thread state into logs; it only requires that adjacent concurrent outputs no longer be merged into a single line because their formatting is exactly identical.

The review raised one limitation: formatting capability and enablement policy must not be conflated. The DEBUG adapter layer can prepare thread-related fields, but whether logs are emitted remains governed by the existing switch. The normal path must not generate more output by default merely because clearer diagnostic text is desired.

There was also discussion of having the native side uniformly concatenate thread identifiers and then reusing them across all upper-layer channels. This direction was not included in the current choice. It expands the local DEBUG requirement to multiple channels that have not been reviewed, and it does not answer who defines the text boundary.

## Current-Round Choice

At present, context attach is treated as a prerequisite for the application callback. Replacement completion, callback dispatch, and callback flag cleanup should be treated as three boundaries to verify separately, rather than using one startup result as a substitute for all judgments. The specific responsibilities of the component factory and ContextImpl can remain under discussion, but "callback first, repair later" is no longer the default path.

thread-aware diagnostic formatting adopts the approach of retaining source context in the adapter layer and remains controlled by the existing debug switch. This choice applies only to the DEBUG adapter layer and does not extend to a unified format for all logging channels.

Items still requiring review: who establishes the visible relationship between the component factory and the outer-object handling of ContextImpl; whether exceptional dispatch enters the same cleanup branch; whether thread-related formatting introduces unnecessary work when logging is disabled. DOC-13 retain the discussion of interface compatibility; this record only documents the callback order and diagnostic text choices.

# Decision Record on Replacement Callbacks and Thread Diagnostics

This record was originally created only for a very narrow handoff question: the point at which a replacement application object counts as having entered the startup chain. thread-aware diagnostic formatting was added later, not because it shares the same implementation with application replacement, but because both issues exposed an old habit: as long as the final state looks normal, assume that every intermediate step was also correct.

This habit does not readily reveal problems during a single startup or single-threaded debugging. The object eventually had a context, the application reached its callback, and the log eventually produced text, so early investigations treated these final states as proof of the sequence. Later reviews separated the issues and found that the final state could not explain what was visible when the callback ran, or which thread the concurrent text originally came from.

## Initial Position Recorded in Year 2023, Month 5

The initial wording took a conservative approach: after the component factory completed the handoff of the replacement object, continue along the old application callback chain as much as possible; if the outer object relationships were later found to be wrong, let the handoff path correct them. The advantage of this direction was its limited scope of changes. At the time, responsibilities among ContextImpl, the component factory, and the replacement object had not yet been clearly divided. Immediately placing attach handling in any one of them would turn a sequencing adjustment into a larger change in responsibility.

There were only two candidates at the time. One was to send the replacement object into the callback first, then attach the outer context afterward; the other was to establish the context needed by the callback first, then send the replacement object into the application lifecycle. The former preserved the shape of the original chain, while the latter required handling object relationships earlier. The early record did not claim that either candidate already covered every entry point, nor did it state that "startup was not interrupted" was a sufficient condition.

The same page initially treated the callback flag as a one-time indication: dispatch had occurred, and some other state update would eventually overwrite it. As a result, the record focused only on whether onCreate was reached, without separately stating when the flag should be cleared. Looking back, this omission was more important than it seemed at the time; it mixed dispatch-time state into subsequent object state.

The DEBUG adapter layer made the same simplification. Diagnostic text was treated as a standalone description of a single invocation, which seemed fine in a single-threaded setting. There was no conclusion at the time about whether the text could still identify each source when multiple threads passed through the formatting path almost simultaneously. The early record left only one question: whether thread-related information was worth including in the formatted result; it did not describe this as a public interface, nor did it change the practice of leaving logging off by default.

## Why That native Path Is Still Here

The old investigation notes led from the issue name and call name to `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/third_party/lss/linux_syscall_support.h`. This came from the local declarations and nearby navigation available at the time. Someone subsequently treated this entry point as a lead on application replacement timing, trying to find the root cause of the callback ordering near the syscall wrapper layer.

That hypothesis did not hold up. The file is still worth retaining: when revisiting the old notes, it provides a starting point for checking the local declarations available at the time; it also explains why the early investigation ended up near a native support header. But a path's location does not establish implementation responsibility. The file's appearance among the old leads does not mean that it determines the relationships among the component factory, ContextImpl, and the application object.

This section was not deleted so that new readers would not encounter only an abrupt "do not look here." The false lead is also part of the background to this decision: it shows that what was missing at the time was observation at the object handoff, not one more neighboring file.

## Review Addendum from Year 2023, Month 12

The counterexample raised in the review was straightforward. The fact that the replacement object has been created does not mean that it can read a stable context in the first application callback. If the callback reads the application context, saves the outer context, or selects a subsequent branch based on the object relationships at its start, correcting those relationships after the callback ends cannot undo the reads that have already occurred.

This reduced the explanatory value of "successful replacement" in the old discussion. The object being replaced, the object being able to use context in the callback, and callback dispatch being complete should be described separately. They do not necessarily happen at the same time.

- The target Application has been produced by the replacement path and has become the object for the subsequent handoff.
- That object already has the context relationships needed for this callback.
- Lifecycle callback dispatch has completed, and dispatch-time state can be cleared.

A successful application startup shows, at most, that the first item has occurred, and may sometimes obscure the second; it does not directly prove that reads inside the callback see stable object relationships. The third item is even less something that can be inferred from the startup result, because whether the callback flag remains is a matter of dispatch-time state, not whether the object ultimately survives.

The review did not directly specify that "the component factory is responsible for attach" or that "ContextImpl is responsible for attach." The record deliberately leaves that open. Rejecting the safety of repairs after the callback does not mean that this page alone can assign responsibility to every neighboring implementation. The decision that can be made here concerns the timing boundary, not which object should contain each line of implementation.

## The Previously Recommended Approach

The following passage comes from an older version. It is retained in its original position and no longer applies:

> Run the replacement object's application callback first; if a context inconsistency is found afterward, let the handoff path correct the outer context. The callback flag can wait to be overwritten by the next state update.

The problem with this approach is not that it "will inevitably crash." Replacement objects that do not read context may be entirely unaffected, so the old path appeared usable in some scenarios. The actual boundary is what has already been read inside the callback. If a read occurs before the repair, obtaining a complete object later cannot make that callback choose its branch again.

The second sentence was also overturned. The callback flag describes the current dispatch window, and responsibility for clearing it should not be passed to the next application startup, another callback, or some unpredictable object update. In particular, when dispatch is interrupted, waiting for a future state to overwrite it is not a cleanup strategy.

The old passage is not retained as a continuing recommendation. It explains why "the final object is correct" was later changed to "the object relationships already support reads when the callback starts." If the old approach were simply erased, readers would see only the added constraint, not the mistaken judgment it addresses.

## A Review Brought the Issue Back to the First Read

The subsequent review did not produce a consistent native failure signature. Attention initially focused on hook, class-name conversion, and call adjacency; these leads helped narrow the inspection scope, but could not answer the earlier timing question: when the replacement object enters onCreate, does it see an environment where attach is already complete, or an intermediate state that will only be completed later.

This also changed the original checking method. The old method usually checked whether the process started and whether it reached the expected callback. Those observations were too coarse to distinguish between a callback using a stable context and one using object relationships that were only repaired after the callback ended. Both cases could leave the same superficial results of "started" and "called."

The review switched to observing three points: first, confirm where the replacement object is first dispatched; then, confirm whether the context needed by the callback is available before that point; finally, independently confirm where the dispatch-time flag is cleared. These are not the same check under three different names. The first identifies the handoff object, the second addresses callback reads, and the third addresses dispatch state.

This round did not expand the various component factory implementations into a compatibility table. The available material supports the boundaries above, not extending the conclusion to entry points that have not appeared. Nor was callback ordering inferred from the native path, because that path can only preserve a historical navigation reference, not account for the reference relationships on the application lifecycle side.

## A Detour in the Formatting Discussion

thread-aware diagnostic formatting was initially seen as a local convenience: include thread-related information alongside the DEBUG text to remove one guess during investigation. After review, that description seemed to understate the issue. Formatted text often becomes detached from its original setting when it is excerpted, saved elsewhere, or forwarded on its own; when multiple threads produce identically formatted content around the same time, readers may mistakenly merge two records into a single call chain.

The first idea was to keep the original format and always return to an external trace when differentiation was needed. This remains useful when the trace is complete, and was not rejected as an investigation technique. But it cannot be the sole basis: what is available is often just a piece of log text, with the external correlation already missing or unavailable for viewing alongside the saved content.

The second idea was to retain thread-related context in the formatting adapter layer, so that a piece of diagnostic text could distinguish its concurrent source on its own. "Thread-related" here does not mean outputting all of a thread's internal state, nor copying trace content into the text. The goal is only to prevent two adjacent threads from being read as one sequence because their formats are identical.

The review did not accept extending this to "therefore all logs must include thread details." The output switch and formatting capability are separate layers. The DEBUG adapter layer can support more distinguishable text, but when logging is off by default, the normal path should not change its output policy because diagnostics might be needed in the future.

There was another proposal that did not become part of the decision: centrally append thread identifiers on the native side for reuse by the various upper-layer channels. This would expand a local DEBUG requirement into multiple channels that had not yet been reviewed, without resolving who was responsible for defining the text boundaries. The current record therefore retains only the adapter-layer direction.

## Two Corrections from the Review Meeting

During one review, someone pointed out the problem with the old judgment in a single sentence: once the callback has read context, correcting the outer context afterward only gives later observers a better final state; it does not make the earlier read never have happened.

That sentence led to a change in wording. What had previously said "it is enough for the final object to be correct" was later changed to "when the callback starts, the object relationships must already support the callback's reads." This change does not require the callback to understand every internal detail of ContextImpl; it requires the replacement handoff path not to send an object into the application lifecycle before attach has occurred.

The other addendum concerned the callback flag. The old notes described cleanup as something like an incidental optimization that could be deferred as long as the next dispatch was unaffected. The review did not accept that description. The flag is part of the current dispatch and should be cleared when that dispatch ends; neither normal return nor interruption paths may leave it to unrelated subsequent object actions.

These corrections did not resolve every implementation question. Exactly who establishes the outer object relationships at the boundary between the component factory and ContextImpl still needs to be specified on the implementation side. What is retained here is the settled ordering condition, along with the old practices that can no longer serve as the default approach.

## Current Decision as of Year 2025, Month 3

The application replacement path first establishes the context relationships needed by the callback, then sends the replacement object into the application callback. Replacement completion, callback dispatch, and callback flag cleanup remain three independently checked boundaries; implementation responsibility can still be discussed, but "callback first, repair later" is no longer available as an equivalent option.

ProxyApplication.onCreate must call JniBridge.ra with the asset application name before JniBridge.craoc and clear the callback flag after dispatch.

This ordering requirement brings the previously separated checks onto the same dispatch boundary: the asset application name is first passed to the replacement entry point, and only then does subsequent callback processing begin; after dispatch ends, the callback flag should no longer remain in the state for that dispatch. It does not say that all startup entry points share the same implementation, nor does it change the handling of logging being off by default.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> AssetApplicationName
    AssetApplicationName --> ReplacementEntry: JniBridge.ra
    ReplacementEntry --> CallbackDispatch: JniBridge.craoc
    CallbackDispatch --> CallbackFlagCleared: after dispatch
    CallbackFlagCleared --> [*]
```

The current scope of thread-aware diagnostic formatting is narrow: when the DEBUG adapter layer is already enabled, formatted results should distinguish concurrent sources, preventing output from adjacent threads from being read as a single call chain. Thread information is context for the diagnostic text, not a replacement for an external trace, and it does not require the application replacement path to depend on diagnostic output.

## Issues Not Yet Split Out

The specific division of responsibility between the component factory and ContextImpl outer object handling still needs to be explained on the implementation side. This page establishes the callback preconditions, rather than fixing every attach detail here. If either side later changes the handoff location, it must still preserve the boundary that context is readable before the callback starts.

Dispatch involving exceptions also remains unresolved. What has been established is that clearing the callback flag must follow the end of the current dispatch and cannot wait for the next normal startup; the existing record is insufficient to establish which protective branch is most appropriate, and an unconfirmed exception-handling approach cannot be presented as an established implementation.

For diagnostic text, whether thread-related formatting still introduces extra work when logging is off requires further examination of the adapter layer's actual paths. The current choice only requires text to distinguish its source when DEBUG is enabled, and does not imply all the details for disabled states.

## Retained Old Examples

### Old Example: Looking Only at the Startup Result

Earlier investigations treated "the process starts and onCreate is called" as proof that the replacement sequence was correct. This example can now show only that the chain did not break immediately. It cannot show that the context read inside onCreate was already stable, nor that the callback flag was cleared after dispatch.

### Old Example: Always Relying on an External trace to Explain Concurrent Text

The old manual recommended always returning to an external trace to determine thread attribution when DEBUG text was identical. When the trace is complete, this remains a useful supporting method; it is not a substitute for readable diagnostic text. Once logs have been excerpted or forwarded independently, the external correlation is often missing.

### Old Navigation

`shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/third_party/lss/linux_syscall_support.h` is still retained as an entry point into the old investigation notes. Checking historical declarations can start here; determining the current callback order still requires following the actual references through the replacement handoff and application lifecycle.

# Replacement, Attachment, and ABI Mapping Proposal

Start by considering application replacement and Context attach separately. The current idea is to make the replacement object available to subsequent initialization only after it is ready; don't treat "can create the replacement object" and "ready to attach the context" as the same completion point.

The other track is the loader's ABI map. The early assessment was that native lookup should be stable as long as the map could select the ABI directory. There are no counterexamples to this assessment yet, but there isn't enough material from callers either, so we're not treating it as an interface commitment yet.

Two small changes to try:

- Keep the ordering inspectable next to the application replacement entry point; don't hide the attach operation inside a loader branch.
- Have the ABI map handle only ABI directory selection; don't combine native asset extraction, search paths, and application replacement in one place.

For the old path, start by tracing back from `shell/src/main/cpp/reflect/android_app_Application.h`. This can help verify application-related declarations and nearby entry points, but it cannot replace a review of the actual startup chain.

The conditions for dropping the trial are simple: if the replacement object can only be obtained after attach, or if the ABI map has to change the application replacement sequence in order to work, this trial split won't work. In that case, leave things as they are and collect a startup trace first.
versions.change_summary: Document the initial split between replacement and the ABI map

# Replacement Attachment and ABI Mapping Proposal

The initial draft framed the problem as two almost independent switches: application replacement on one side, and the loader ABI map on the other. After review, that framing is too weak. They indeed should not take on each other's responsibilities, but both appear during startup; one may expose state too early, while the other may cause an error to be interpreted as a native directory-selection problem.

Let us retain the conclusion from the initial draft: the ABI map should not be responsible for creating or attaching application objects. Its input should be already-determined ABI information, and its output should serve only ABI directory selection. Putting ContextImpl, the component factory, or Context attach into the map-selection process would make a single ABI regression rewrite the Java startup boundary as well, and during investigation it would be impossible to tell whether the directory was not selected or the replacement object appeared too late.

But retract the initial draft's other statement, "As long as the map can select a directory, searching will be stable." A selected directory does not mean the native asset is already available; the extraction strategy, whether the archive retains the required content, and whether the final native search path accepts that directory are still separate questions. This proposal has no evidence that they have a fixed order, much less evidence to present them as the compatibility definition of the loader ABI map.

## Boundary to test this time

On the application-replacement side, we discuss only two observable points: when the replacement object is complete, and the point after which Context attach occurs. Here, "complete" does not mean that the object has been allocated; it means that subsequent startup code can continue executing with it as the application object. If the object has already been created but attach is still entered with the old object, replacement exists at the interface level, but the actual boundary has not moved.

On the loader side, we discuss only whether the ABI map can preserve the existing directory selection with the same package contents. Compatibility does not mean that all ABI cases produce the same result; it means that an existing ABI selection is not redirected to another directory by map integration, and that an uncovered ABI does not silently fall back to a seemingly usable default directory. When there is no explicit match, failure or unresolved status should be retained rather than papered over by application initialization.

The intersection of these two lines is not "who calls whom first," but the diagnostic entry point. When startup fails, first check whether the replacement object has already crossed Context attach, then check whether the directory provided by the ABI map is included in native search. This at least lets us separate Java startup ordering from the native search path as two types of problems. DOC-14 documents on-site troubleshooting of debug CLI state and ABI-specific native search path; we do not reproduce that troubleshooting tree here.

## Candidate approaches

**Candidate A: Keep the existing replacement entry point and add only ordering checks before and after the entry point.** This involves little change and is suitable for first confirming whether replacement is observed too early or too late. The drawback is that it cannot explain loader-map compatibility; once native loading fails, we still need to find path evidence elsewhere.

**Candidate B: Move application replacement to before Context attach and keep the ABI map as an independent selector.** This is the current preference. The benefit is that the interface responsibilities are fairly clear: the replacement logic does not need to know the ABI directory, and the map does not need to hold application state. The cost is that old callers which treat attach as the signal that replacement is complete will see a timing change.

**Candidate C: Have the loader temporarily trigger application replacement when a native path is needed.** The initial draft treated this as a way to reduce the number of entry points. We no longer recommend continuing with it. It couples the loader's failure behavior to the application lifecycle and also makes anomalies in the ABI-specific search path look like ContextImpl issues.

Candidate B is still only a trial, not a claim about all startup paths. The component factory, Manifest attributes, and debug CLI may all provide different entry points; the current material does not support reducing them to a single call chain. Any change that needs to pass through these entry points must record the caller-side results separately.

## Review method

The review starts with `shell/src/main/cpp/reflect/android_app_Application.h`, treating it only as a navigation point for application-related declarations. First confirm whether the replacement and attach actions can be distinguished at the observation points; then record native-loading-related failures separately, to avoid attributing an error to the ABI map.

The minimum set of results to retain is not a large, comprehensive startup log, but three items: when the replacement object becomes visible, which application object is used before and after Context attach, and which directory the ABI map ultimately selected. If the third item is missing, we cannot infer map compatibility from native success or failure; if the first two are missing, we cannot infer that the replacement timing was correct from loader success.

For packages with multiple ABI variants, the trial compares only "the directory that would originally have been selected" with "the directory selected after map integration." Do not fabricate a compatibility result for ABI not included in the map. For a package with a single ABI variant, likewise do not skip recording just because there is only one directory: a single directory can only reduce the selection branches; it cannot prove that the native asset has been extracted or that the search path has accepted it.

## Risks remaining for now

The easiest thing to overlook is when old callers observe the state. If a caller reads the application before attach, it may still receive the old object; if it reads only after attach, the earlier replacement may appear to have made no difference. Neither outcome alone indicates whether the approach is right or wrong; we must first know which point the caller treats as the stable boundary.

Another risk is treating archive contents, native asset extraction, and the ABI directory as the same layer. They often occur together, but they do not necessarily fail together. During the trial, "can load" is not the sole pass criterion; as long as directory selection is correct but the asset is missing, it should remain classified as an asset-side or archive-side issue.

The initial draft did not specify what to do to recover after a rollback; add it here: once Candidate B changes the pre-attach state relied on by existing callers, first roll back the timing move while retaining the independent selection experiment for the ABI map; once the map causes an existing ABI to point to a different directory, stop integrating the map, return to the original directory selection, and record the mapping difference separately. Do not use a temporary application callback to compensate for a loader directory error.

There are still two unconfirmed items: whether the component-factory entry point shares the same observation point as the current replacement entry point; and whether legacy native search uses an implicit directory when there is no matching ABI. The former requires a startup trace, and the latter requires actual artifacts and load results.
versions.change_summary: Separated object handoff from directory selection after review.

# Replacement, Attachment, and ABI Mapping Proposal

This page was originally retained because there were two very similar calls to do something "earlier" in the startup flow: some said application replacement needed to happen earlier, while others said the loader needed to select the ABI directory earlier too. Early discussions wrote them side by side, and they were later mistaken for the same kind of change. Looking back, what they share is a startup window, not implementation responsibility.

The old draft has not been deleted. It still reminds investigators that a native loading error need not be attributed to application replacement as the first explanation; when the application object is wrong, the loader's output should not be expected to explain it either. However, the old draft overstated the role of the ABI map, treating "a directory has been selected" as roughly equivalent to "the native path is already usable". That assessment is no longer suitable as a basis for integration.

What is retained here consists of proposals raised during interface review, withdrawn inferences, and boundaries still worth revisiting. Callers, build artifacts, and routine troubleshooting entry points each have their own records. DOC-14 contains field notes on debug CLI state and the ABI-specific native search path; this page does not repeat those branches.

## The Starting Point at the Time

The initial working assumption was straightforward: if application replacement happened before Context attach, subsequent startup code would not need to guess the state during the gap when "the old object is already attached, but the new object has not yet taken over". This assumption concerns only the object handoff. It does not require the loader to know about ContextImpl, nor does it require native directory selection to participate in the application lifecycle.

Around the same time, the loader ABI map was proposed as the central point for directory selection. Here, the map is a selection relationship that points a known ABI to the corresponding ABI directory, not a master switch that fulfills all native runtime requirements. It cannot replace native asset extraction, cannot decide what is retained in the archive, and cannot substitute for acceptance of that directory by the final native search path.

The early text referred to both as "startup compatibility". This created an unnecessary association for readers: as though correct application replacement timing should ensure ABI map compatibility, or a correct map could establish that replacement had no problems. Later review did not support this linkage. This misreading remains in the old paragraphs because it can easily recur when looking at only a snippet of failure output.

## The Abandoned Combined Entry Point

The old proposal tried to reduce observation points: when the loader needed a native path, it would also confirm whether the application had been replaced; when application replacement ran, it would also decide on the ABI directory. Its appeal was that there appeared to be only one startup entry point, and testing seemingly needed to cover it only once.

This proposal was later abandoned, not because having fewer entry points is inherently wrong, but because it collapsed two kinds of failure into one result. When directory selection was wrong, the records would appear near application-related paths; when object replacement happened too late, investigators might mistakenly think the native loading branch had changed the state. Once both were compensated for within the same logic, callers had difficulty distinguishing which old behavior to preserve.

It also implied an unproven premise: every startup path that enters native search passes through the same application replacement point. The available material has not established this premise. Component factories, Manifest attributes, debug entry points, and ordinary startup code may observe different stages; without results from callers, consolidating them into one path would only broaden the scope of the changes.

The old proposal is therefore marked as abandoned, but it has not been erased from the record. It explains why later work insisted on separating "object takeover" from "directory selection", and why the loader must not become a side entry point into the application lifecycle merely to make ordering checks convenient.

## Two Questions Left by the Review

The first question is not "whether replacement is early enough", but "after which point downstream code is allowed to treat the application as a stable object". If the replacement object has been created, but Context attach still uses the old object, successful creation does not mean the handoff is complete. Conversely, if attach has already begun when the replacement only becomes visible, subsequent code has passed through an inconsistent phase even if it eventually obtains the new object.

The second question is not "whether the ABI map exists", but "whether it silently overwrites existing selections". Compatibility should be assessed against directory selection for existing ABI: a directory that could previously be selected should not switch to another directory without cause after map integration; a ABI with no explicit match should not be forced into a default directory for convenience and presented as a success.

Both questions can arise during the same startup, but they require different records. Object handoff requires identifying the relative positions of replacement and Context attach. Directory selection requires identifying the input to the ABI map and the final directory. Successful native loading is only a subsequent outcome; it cannot be used to infer that the first two conditions have been met.

An early version treated "startup can continue" as sufficiently strong evidence, and that assessment should also be withdrawn. Startup may continue simply because the current device, current ABI, or current package contents did not trigger the gap; it does not establish whether old callers depend on the pre-attach state, nor whether archive retention, native asset extraction, and search paths will change for other packages.

## Boundaries Still Under Trial

The application replacement side only adjusts or checks the ordering of the object handoff. It does not take a ABI name, a ABI directory, or a native asset as a parameter, nor does it treat loader success as proof that replacement is complete. If an implementation must read the ABI map to determine whether the application can be replaced, work should first stop at the interface design stage rather than carrying this coupling into the startup branch.

The loader ABI map side handles only directory selection. It can receive ABI information and provide the corresponding directory; it is not responsible for creating the application, does not hold ContextImpl state, and certainly should not trigger Context attach or write back the application object when a directory is missing. Leaving an unmatched input unmatched makes compatibility breaks easier to find than choosing a directory on the fly.

This separation does not mean that native paths and the application can never have a runtime relationship. It only specifies that, during review, they must not be designed as recovery mechanisms for each other. A native search failure can occur after replacement has completed correctly; likewise, an application object inconsistency can occur on a startup path in which the ABI map plays no part at all.

The same boundary applies to single-ABI packages. Having only one candidate directory reduces the map's selection branches, but does not automatically prove that the native asset exists in that directory, much less that the final search path accepts that location. For multi-ABI packages, the comparison should focus on whether the selected directory remains the same before and after integration, not on labeling the result for every ABI with the same "loading succeeded" outcome.

## Correction to the Ordering

This page previously said only that "replacement should precede attach", without clearly stating an actionable interface sequence. As a result, some interpreted it as "as early as possible", while others understood that the loader could insert a replacement at any point before or after attach. The requirement after review is as follows:

During startup JniBridge.ra must complete before JniBridge.craa so application replacement precedes context attachment.

This statement specifies the completion order of these two interface actions during startup. It does not include the loader ABI map in the call sequence, nor does it elevate native asset extraction, archive retention, or debug switches into the same ordering requirement. The old draft's claim that "putting the loader-side check into the replacement entry point also guarantees the timing" is inconsistent with this requirement and no longer applies.

The emphasis on complete is intended to prevent judging the order solely on the basis that "the replacement branch has already been entered". Entering the branch, allocating the object, and completing the handoff are not the same thing. If JniBridge.ra has not yet completed, JniBridge.craa should not become the starting point for downstream observation of application state. The local steps involved in reaching the completion point still need to be verified against the corresponding source code and callers.

## Rechecking and Observation

`shell/src/main/cpp/reflect/android_app_Application.h` remains a local entry point left by the old troubleshooting records. It is useful for navigating from terms such as application, context, and attach back to declarations and nearby navigation, especially when checking the JniBridge boundary. It is not a complete startup flow diagram, nor should it be read as identifying where the loader ABI map is implemented.

When rechecking, first find a point that distinguishes completion of JniBridge.ra from the start of JniBridge.craa. If only a combined "initialization complete" marker is visible, the records are still insufficient to determine the order. Then check the loader side to confirm whether the ABI map produces only a directory selection. The two observation points do not need to be in the same file or maintained by the same module.

If you encounter ContextImpl outer context reflection or component factory-related code, do not incorporate it into this proposal's ordering conclusions merely because the names are similar. It may be an adjacent implementation or a different entry point. It should be included as material for this trial only when the call relationships show that it directly participates in these two JniBridge actions.

The trial does not require collecting all startup information at once, but each run must answer at least one clearly defined question. For replacement, record whether the application object is handed over before or after JniBridge.ra completes, and on which side of the boundary JniBridge.craa lies. For the ABI map, record the directory selected for a given ABI, and whether it changes before and after integration. Record the two questions separately rather than concluding with a vague "startup is normal".

If an error occurs on the replacement side while the ABI map output remains unchanged, keep the investigation focused on the object handoff and Context attach paths first. Conversely, if the ABI map selection changes while replacement ordering still meets the requirement, first check the directory mapping and its callers rather than using JniBridge timing to explain the directory difference.

When native search fails, first distinguish three things: whether the directory was selected by the map, whether the required native asset is already available in that directory, and whether the search path actually accepts that directory. They may happen in sequence, but they are not the same determination. The old draft compressed them into "the map is incompatible", which was a misattribution.

## Compatibility and Rollback

The benefit of the current trial is a narrower failure surface: application replacement ordering issues can be reproduced independently, and ABI map directory selection issues can also be compared independently. The cost is that old callers treating the pre-attach application as a stable object will expose previously hidden assumptions; old loaders that depend on implicit directory fallback will also appear stricter after map integration.

When the former situation is found, roll back the timing change or the corresponding caller changes rather than replacing the application again through a loader branch. When the latter situation is found, roll back the ABI map integration or directory mapping changes rather than having application replacement choose a fallback directory for native search. Keep the two rollback actions independent so that the next regression test does not return to the combined entry point.

"Preserve failure when there is no matching ABI" is the current proposal's preference, not an indication that all ways of presenting errors have already been defined. The available material provides neither unified error messages nor fallback contracts for each caller. Whether component factory-related entry points bypass the current observation points, and whether old loaders use an implicit directory when there is no matching ABI, still need to be confirmed from startup traces, actual artifacts, and loading results.

# Component Factory and Asset Extraction Migration Procedure

This page separates two issues from a runtime compatibility check that are easy to conflate: startup changes after component factory integration, and extraction of native assets from the package. They come up in the same packaging run, but should not be treated as a single issue during recovery.

The initial assessment placed the component factory on the application replacement side. During migration, preserve the old startup entry point first; after integrating the new path, look only at startup-side changes. If startup does not behave as expected, first return to the original component factory entry path, then verify the timing of application replacement. ContextImpl, the component factory, and application replacement were recorded at the time as three adjacent observation points. A single startup failure is not enough to treat them as one fault point.

Native asset extraction has a separate recovery path. If the extracted libraries are unusable, first restore the pre-migration asset handling, then inspect the ABI directory. The ABI directory can help locate adjacent contents within the package, but does not by itself show that extraction has completed. Early inspection notes tended to list "the directory is still there" as a positive sign. That only indicates that further checks are needed; it cannot substitute for the extraction result.

The sequence used at the time was:

1. Preserve the old startup entry point and confirm that startup still works after restoring it.
2. Integrate the component factory path, recording only startup-side observations and the timing of application replacement.
3. Handle native assets independently; if something goes wrong, restore the old extraction handling without reverting the component factory changes.
4. If both sides have issues, first record clearly which side was restored first, then check whether the issue on the other side persists.

A brief note in the margin says: don't touch the component factory first just because there is a native asset issue. This is not a conclusion about the cause, just a way to avoid changing both paths in one rollback. If both are reverted at once, it will be impossible afterward to tell whether the startup change came from the component factory or asset extraction behavior.

`shell/src/main/cpp/dpt.h` was left as a navigation point in the old investigation notes. All we know at this stage is that it is near what was being discussed at the time; no conclusion has yet been drawn from it about exactly where option parsing, application replacement, or native asset handling belongs.

To add: whether the old asset extraction path is still affected by the timing of application replacement after it has been restored.

# Component Factory and Asset Extraction Migration Workflow

This record continues to keep two migration tracks. The component factory covers the switch state at startup; native asset handling covers extracting packaged contents and their usability afterward. They were raised in the same round of compatibility checks, but that does not mean a single release toggle can validate both, or that a single rollback should cover both.

## Recovery Order Retained from the First Draft

The notes from 2023 roughly divided the problems into "startup entry point" and "the library didn't show up." That division was not detailed enough, but the recovery order is still usable: first make sure the old startup entry point can be restored; if there is an asset issue, restore the old extraction handling first. This at least avoids changing how packaged contents are handled just because a symptom appears on the startup side.

One judgment from the first draft is retained but now marked as outdated: once the old startup entry point has been successfully restored, the component factory switch can be considered complete. That judgment only indicates that the startup symptom has been suppressed. It does not establish whether the switch state was entered correctly, and it leaves no record of where the command-line entry point should be checked.

Another old judgment also needs to retain its original meaning: if the ABI directory looks normal, asset handling can initially be left alone. This was shorthand from a manual inspection. The directory is only one item to revisit on the asset side; it cannot replace an assessment of the extraction stage and its result. Old release notes may still use this wording, so it is not being deleted, but it is no longer a basis for declaring the migration complete.

## The Split Identified During Review

Follow-up review started near `shell/src/main/cpp/dpt.h`. The old record provides this path as a navigation hint to the surrounding area: issue names and call names had led the investigation here. It is not proof of implementation ownership. To investigate further, check the references within the relevant revision; do not infer solely from the header file's directory that the component factory, option parsing, and native asset extraction are all handled there.

Two approaches were compared at the time.

The first was to put the component factory switch and asset handling into the same round of changes, checking only whether the application could start before and after release. It looked simpler: if an issue occurred, all of the old runtime handling could be restored. But this approach left no useful distinction between the outcomes. After the restore, there was no way to tell whether the startup side had recovered or the asset-side change had just happened to be reverted; the next migration would require separating them again.

The second was to keep two checkpoints. On the component factory side, check the startup entry point and switch state; on the native asset side, check whether the contents enter extraction and whether an issue occurs during extraction or afterward. If a problem occurs, restore only the corresponding old path. The second approach was adopted because it allows later records to retain results for each side, rather than just "the application starts after the restore."

```text
Before migration
  Startup entry point   -> Original component factory entry method
  Packaged native asset -> Original extraction handling

After migration
  Startup entry point   -> Component factory switch state
  Packaged native asset -> extraction handling

When an issue occurs
  Startup side          -> Restore the old startup entry point
  asset side            -> Restore the old extraction handling
```

The two lines in the diagram represent operational boundaries; they do not imply that the two paths share the same implementation object. The old notes drew them as a continuous chain, making it easy to read a causal relationship into symptoms occurring close together in time.

## A Joint Pass Criterion That Did Not Work

During review, "the application can start and the packaged contents still exist" was tried as a joint pass criterion. This criterion was later discontinued.

The problem is that contents being present in the package, contents being extracted, and the extracted result being usable are three different observations. Collapsing them into "asset is OK" loses the location of the issue. Likewise, the application being able to start does not mean the component factory switch state has been confirmed. Putting two surface-level results side by side does not supply the information missing from either checkpoint.

After this attempt, the record was changed to identify the location first, then determine the recovery action:

- For startup issues or an unclear switch state, return to the startup side first; leave asset handling unchanged.
- If a native asset issue occurs during extraction, return to the old extraction handling first; leave the component factory unchanged.
- If the result is found to be unusable only after extraction, first record it separately from issues during extraction, then revisit nearby items such as the ABI directory.
- If symptoms appear on both sides at the same time, restore each item in turn and record the results separately; do not perform a full rollback in one step.

This does not mean the two tracks cannot affect each other. The existing records do not prove that they have no shared prerequisites; they only establish that one side cannot be treated as the cause of the other without observations specific to that side.

## Review Addendum

During review, it was proposed that the component factory state should be directly checkable, rather than inferred only from startup results. This replaced the old "if it starts, it passes" criterion. The native asset side also retains its own place in the record: release checks must record the stage of failure and downloadable artifacts separately, to avoid recording continued artifact availability as completed extraction.

Therefore, keep both old paths initially during migration. If a problem occurs on the component factory side, restore the original startup entry point; if a problem occurs on the native asset side, restore the pre-migration extraction handling. Once the restore is complete, record only the changes on that side; do not add a passing conclusion for the other side based on its normal behavior.

Whether the timing of application replacement and the timing of native asset extraction share any prerequisites remains unconfirmed. This question remains open here; the earlier practice of answering it with a single startup result is no longer supportable.
