# Native Class Name Slash Conversion Migration Process

This migration concerns the verification entry points and comparison records, not moving a seemingly similar native string-processing snippet into R42. The old artifact remains as the baseline. R42 candidates are replaced for the corresponding batch only when they can be rechecked at the same class-name string boundary. The earlier clues came from the issue name, call name, and file path; during review, handle these three separately.

````text
Original class name in the old artifact
        |
        v
Native boundary of the old caller
        |
        v
Old conversion result  ───────> Retained for comparison

The same input in the R42 candidate
        |
        v
Confirmed native boundary
        |
        v
R42 conversion result ──────> Compared with the old result
````

The diagram above only shows the recording order; it does not mean that `linux_syscall_support.h` necessarily has a conversion implementation. This file is the currently available local navigation entry; the actual relationship still needs to be determined from `internal/aegis-runtime`'s `v_prev` references.

## Establish one comparable record first

One row in the migration table corresponds to one passage from the caller to the native boundary. At least four values must be retained: the class name before entering the boundary, where the conversion occurs, the converted value, and the call site that the value subsequently enters. If any of these is missing, all that can be said is "a similar output was seen"; the two sides cannot be called the same path.

The old artifact's input must be preserved as-is. Do not first change the class name to the expected format and then begin the review, or the boundary before conversion will be lost. The R42 candidate must also accept the same raw input; if the candidate has already changed the string at an earlier location, record that location instead of treating the changed value as the raw value.

"Did not reach the conversion point" and "reached the conversion point but produced the same result" must be written separately. The former means it was not reached; only the latter has comparable output. Even if the final strings on both sides are the same, that does not confirm that the paths are the same, because one value may be processed at the caller while the other may be processed only at the native boundary.

The conversion direction, whether repeated conversion is allowed, and where exceptional input ends up must all be determined by the entry point in the actual references. A filename containing terms such as native or class name can only help with locating it; it cannot replace the call relationship. When the entry point cannot temporarily be found, leave it unknown rather than inferring a rule from the name.

## File entry point and old path

The frozen navigation location is:

`internal/aegis-runtime` / `v_prev` / `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/third_party/lss/linux_syscall_support.h`

When using it, first inspect the local declarations, then inspect the actual references connected to the class-name string. If the references do not connect that header file to the class-name boundary, record "entry point unverified" and continue from the caller already found. Related declarations near the header file do not mean that all native class names pass through here, nor that this is the final conversion location.

Old investigation records once pointed the issue name and call name directly to this file. That pointer still has navigational value, but it cannot by itself determine the migration. The initial draft made "find the conversion location from this file" the default step, which mistakes the file location for implementation ownership. Now retain this path as the starting point for tracing back, and change the criterion to whether the actual references can connect the caller, string, and native boundary.

If this file has no match but the caller and boundary can already be aligned, there is no need to fill in an assumed conversion point just to keep the path consistent. Conversely, seeing only a file match without a caller is not enough to put the row into a completed batch.

## Switch from the old entry to R42

Batches are divided by caller and observed boundaries, not by directory or filename. Multiple inputs from the same caller can be placed in one batch; two callers must be kept separate even if they produce the same string. Batch sizes do not need to be consistent; what is recorded is the relationship that can already be rechecked.

The first batch accepts only callers for which the raw input and call location can be obtained on both sides. Write each row in this order:

1. Retrieve the unprocessed class name from the old artifact and record its location before it enters the native boundary.
2. Have the R42 candidate accept the same input; do not replace the caller or adjust the string in advance.
3. Mark the pre-conversion value, post-conversion value, and actual call site separately.
4. Compare the value received by the call site and note whether the boundaries match.
5. Save the old record and candidate record; if the call chain is later found to have changed, trace back from this row.

Records with the same value but different boundaries are marked "results comparable, path under investigation" and do not count as complete. Do not immediately attribute records with different values to slash conversion either; first identify whether the difference appears before, during, or after conversion. If only the native side can be observed, retain "candidate visible, caller not aligned" and do not turn this record into migration authorization.

The second batch is for callers that the first batch cannot cover. A common situation is that the old artifact's record stops at one call site while the R42 candidate's record appears earlier or later. In that case, fill in the call relationship first, then compare the strings. A seemingly identical output cannot be used to replace a missing boundary.

Keep counterexamples in their owning batch. A counterexample is not a set of bad names detached from the caller; it should include the raw input, observation location, and problematic value together. If only the converted string is retained, the next review cannot determine whether the difference came from the caller, the native boundary, or a downstream consumer.

## Several checkpoints during migration

Records ready to switch must simultaneously meet these observed conditions: both the old artifact and the R42 candidate have the raw input; the callers on both sides can be matched; the locations before and after conversion have been written down; and the comparison does not depend on additional manual preprocessing. If any one item is missing, continue using the old artifact as the comparison entry point.

Completion of the candidate build itself is not a batch-switch signal. The switch applies only to rows that have already been reviewed; all old paths cannot be replaced at once. When switching, append the candidate-side references, boundary, and comparison result without overwriting the old record. This makes it possible to see both the input left by the old artifact at the time and the location at which the R42 candidate processed it.

If it is later discovered that the candidate bypassed the conversion point that was originally assumed, move the batch back to under investigation. Do not rewrite the old result or replace the old artifact's record with a new assumption. If the old record lacks the raw input, keep that batch on the old path as well and supplement the raw value first.

Restore the batch's old entry in the following situations:

- The candidate side cannot reproduce the old caller's raw input;
- The values on the two sides differ, but it is still impossible to identify the stage where the difference occurred;
- A declaration exists near the header file, but there is no actual call-chain reference;
- The class name must be manually rewritten before entering native in order to obtain the same result.

Restoring is not deleting the candidate record. Retain the failed input, observed boundary, and references used, and return the batch to the old path. The next review should continue from the location of the difference rather than reconstructing the sample.

## Counterexamples and compatibility assessment

The presence of a slash in a class name does not automatically mean that compatibility conversion has been completed. To determine whether a record can be migrated, first see where the raw value comes from, then see which call site consumes the converted result. If the caller already provides a certain format, it must still be recorded as-is; do not overwrite it with the expected format. The possibility of repeated conversion must also remain in the specific call chain; it cannot be inferred directly from the name "slash conversion".

If the results from the old artifact and candidate side are the same, but one is processed at the caller and the other at the native boundary, the migration record should retain both paths. They can be used for result comparison, but they cannot be merged into the same call relationship. If the difference occurs in a downstream consumer, first mark the native boundary as consistent, then mark the downstream location as under investigation; do not attribute all differences to the conversion step.

What can currently be confirmed is that the verification method needs to center on the raw input, caller, native boundary, and call site. What cannot currently be confirmed from the file location is ownership of the conversion implementation, the complete set of callers, and the stage at which each counterexample occurred. Attach these unknowns separately to the specific batches rather than merging them into a global string rule.

## Preservation and correction of the old determination

The sequence left in the initial draft is "find the conversion location from `linux_syscall_support.h`, then replace them one by one". This determination remains in the historical record, but it is no longer an execution step. The reviewed sequence is to find the caller first, then confirm the native boundary, and finally return to the area near the file to verify declarations and adjacency relationships.

The old path is still useful because it retains the local entry points for the issue name, call name, and current revision. It is no longer treated as proof of implementation ownership. When the file has no match, it does not block verification of a caller that has already been found; when the file does have a match, it likewise does not mean that class-name conversion definitely occurs there.

When each record is completed, update only the corresponding batch. Do not use one batch's result to replace the status of other callers, and do not mark a record as passed if its raw input has not yet been found. The switching scope of R42 grows as more rows are reviewed; unaligned callers remain at the old entry.

The specific items not yet closed out are the callers that actually need to enter batches, the conversion direction of each chain, and the locations of counterexamples in the old artifact that still lack raw input. Keep them unconfirmed, and fill in whichever item is found next.

# Release Automation Handoff Troubleshooting Tree

Use this tree when the current entry point still shows the processing status of dpt · Release Automation but processing hasn't progressed, or when the page shows only information such as an exit action or a permissions message. Don't retry yet. An earlier record documents a premature retry that overwrote the first failure sample with the later result, leaving no way to compare the differences between the two environments afterward.

First, capture what you can see in one place: the exact text displayed at the entry point, the artifact version involved, whether the build queue is still changing, whether the exit action is still available, and how this attempt's environment differs from the previous one. Keep only the first failure sample; start a separate record for subsequent actions. The entry path is `docs/adj-dpt/runbooks/dpt-release-automation-escalation-contacts.md`.

The processing status at the entry point is just the starting point for choosing a branch, not a determination of the release outcome. First check whether the entry point opens, then whether the build queue is changing, and only then deal with any exit action still displayed on the page. If you lack evidence for the preceding check, don't connect later observations into a single cause. In particular, don't assume that the artifact version has already entered the withdrawal window just because the exit action is still present.

## Entry Point Unavailable

**The entry point won't open, or only shows permissions-related messages.**

Don't conclude from this that the release has failed. Hand this off to the permissions owner first, with the exact text from the entry point and the access environment. Keep the permissions message verbatim; writing only "won't open" would conflate an access issue with the processing status of dpt-release-automation. The permissions owner handles only access and authorization to perform actions; they cannot assess the build queue or artifact status in place of the automation side.

Until permissions are confirmed, don't perform the exit action on their behalf or record the artifact version as withdrawn. If an exit action is still visible on the page, that only shows that the current viewer can see that entry point; it doesn't establish that the action can be executed for the current version. If you can't confirm which version the action applies to, stay on this branch. Don't fill in the gap with the version shown on an old page.

If the processing status becomes visible again after access is restored, return to the automation branch below and continue from the first failure sample. There's no need to carry out actions previously considered on speculation, and don't overwrite the original permissions message with the page shown after access is restored. The two samples can be kept side by side: one shows access to the entry point, and the other shows whether processing continued.

## Queue Not Changing

**The entry point opens and dpt-release-automation is shown as processing, but the build queue has no new changes.**

Hand the sample to dpt-release-automation: retain what the entry point displays, the artifact version, and the state when the queue stopped changing. Make clear in the handoff that there are no new changes in the queue, rather than simply calling it a build failure. The available material supports only the former conclusion; "stuck" on the page cannot stand in for a conclusion that a particular build step has failed.

First verify whether the queue really stayed unchanged during the observation period. If the entry point hasn't refreshed but the queue is still changing, record this as a mismatch between the entry point display and the queue state. Don't use the exit action or hand it off to the permissions owner. Continue to retain the earliest sample of this mismatch; don't switch environments and rerun just to get the entry point displaying again.

If the maintainer asks for new input, pause here first. You can add the current entry point location and the existing samples, but don't execute the exit action first to create a second state. Changes to the page after exiting can only show what the exit action affected, not why the queue stopped changing.

## Processing Stopped and Exit Action Still Present

**The entry point shows that processing has stopped, and the exit action is still present.**

First confirm that the exit action applies to the artifact version currently displayed. Don't reuse the conclusion from the previous page view. If you can't confirm the version, don't execute the action. What needs to be retained here is not "there's a clickable button," but whether the exit action can be tied to the current version; if that link is missing, later records won't be able to show what the withdrawal window actually affected.

You can use the exit action to exit the current processing flow, but before executing it, retain the first failure sample, the version, and the environment differences. After exiting, record whether the entry point still retains that version and whether the withdrawal window has changed. Describe only what was visible before and after the action. Don't use the record to infer why processing originally got stuck, or report a successful exit as automation having recovered.

If the exit action is unavailable, reports insufficient permissions, or you can't confirm which version it applies to, don't execute it. Hand it off through the permissions branch and note "exit action cannot be confirmed" in the handoff. If the entry point also shows that the queue hasn't changed, the queue sample still goes to dpt-release-automation; the permissions message must not override that observation.

## What to Include in the Handoff

The handoff to dpt-release-automation only needs to include: what the entry point currently displays, the first failure sample, the artifact version, whether the build queue is changing, environment differences, and whether the exit action has already been attempted. If it hasn't, just write that it hasn't been attempted; don't fill the gap with a hypothetical recovery result. The automation side needs to know the visible point where processing stopped, not speculation that mixes permissions, exiting, and the queue together.

Include only messages related to access or authorization to perform actions in the handoff to the permissions owner, along with the same entry point location. If the issue is with the exit action, just state whether the action is unavailable or permission is denied. Keep the artifact version, whether the queue is changing, and similar details in the automation branch to avoid treating both handoff recipients as the final authority on the same observation.

If neither side has new evidence, the tree stops at the current node. Keep the old assessment and the new sample side by side. After the maintainers reply, update only the corresponding item; there's no need to rewrite the other branch at the same time. Recovery actions in the shared environment have not yet been verified.

# Caller Integration Test Window Closeout Checklist

This page is still here because when a window ends, someone always looks in the old checklist for the last output. It records the closeout action for one gradle · Caller Integration, not a release rule that every project can copy later. The earliest version treated the current entry point as stable; in actual use, treat it first as something to verify. If it still points to an old value after the window ends, that does not automatically mean replacement failed.

The old version's original wording has not been deleted:

> Do not clear the working setup after seeing archive metadata.
>
> If `Apply replacement` does not appear, stop here.

These two lines were useful at the time because the borrowed entry point and final output were often cleared together. They also left a misleading implication: archive metadata can only indicate that someone left archival information; it cannot prove that the current revision has been replaced, much less stand in for the actual result of the last gradle-client-integration. Later checks add this distinction, but do not rewrite the old lines into a new conclusion.

During the window, a very small written record is enough: what was borrowed, the latest return time, where the last execution is kept, and which old value to return to during rollback. Here, "borrowed" can mean a temporary account, worker, environment, or proxy; if nothing was actually borrowed, do not invent a name just to fill in the form. The point is that, before closeout, someone can determine which things need to be revoked and which are merely output from this run.

| Record item | Content to leave before closeout |
| --- | --- |
| Current entry point | The revision the entry point targets at the end of the window, or a status that still cannot be determined |
| Last output | Exit code, the gradle · Caller Integration identifier, and the last log segment |
| Borrowed items | The items actually borrowed from the temporary account, worker, environment, or proxy options, and the return time |
| Rollback entry point | The old value or a known rollback location; if there is no old value, mark it blank directly |

"Mark it blank" is not an omission. An earlier execution record belonged to the previous version, while the current result had no source attached; this cannot be filled in by copying the old record. If there is only one old execution record in the window, store it separately from the current result first, then continue judging. Writing the previous version as a success path will cause later comparisons to mistake old input for current input.

## When opening the window

- [ ] Fix this run's `gradle-client-integration`, current entry point, and execution command. If any one of them can only be inferred from the old cache, write "inferred" in the record; do not write it as a fixed input.
- [ ] Leave one sample that can complete successfully, and one that is rejected or stopped partway through. The two samples do not need to cover all combinations; they only explain what normal completion and an expected stop mean in this window.
- [ ] When temporary conditions are borrowed, write down the latest return time. Do not carry temporary conditions with no return time into the closeout stage.
- [ ] Save the inputs and version before the first execution. If you later modify the setup for diagnosis, mark the new green result separately from the original result; do not use it to overwrite the original failed sample.

This once said, "Finish the success path first, then inspect the rejection path." That saves time in a short window, but when the revisions on the two sides of gradle-client-integration do not match, this order hides the first divergence. The retained approach now is: after fixing the command and current entry point, replace only the current revision and do not adjust the other inputs along with it. DPTC-006 are pointers left for this single-variable rerun; they are not a requirement to rerun a round at every closeout.

If, after fixing the conditions, it is still impossible to tell whether the current entry point came from the old cache or an old task, stop the replacement action. Keep the window-end timestamp, current entry point, and last output, and instead check the cache or task; do not clean up first and then wait for an explanation. The records in DPTC-008 are exactly this situation: the window ended, the entry point was still the old value, and confirming where the old value came from was more important than continuing the replacement.

## A Few Easily Confused Points in the Middle of the Window

"Last output" is not the last log line that displays success. At a minimum, put the exit code, the caller integration-test identifier, and the last log segment together; otherwise, after returning the current revision, later readers can see only a piece of text detached from its input. DPTC-003 use this closeout approach: follow the execution record to the first broken link and stop at the current result, without filling in a complete cause for it.

The current entry point is not the only comparison object either. When the two records differ, first compare the generation commands and timestamps, and stop at the first divergence. DPTC-013 can serve as navigation for this kind of incident. This does not mean the two records necessarily came from the same worker, nor does it require combining the two logs into one; as long as the first divergence remains, later matching output has no explanatory value.

When version synchronization lags, the old value can temporarily remain as the rollback entry point. DPTC-001 were once work items for this, but the work was later moved to an offline window, and the card itself no longer remains on the board. This historical status does not mean that the old value has been verified as rollback-safe. At closeout, write "old value ready for use" or "old value has been restored to the entry point"; do not combine the two into one status.

The following is an abbreviated version of the old wording, retained for comparison:

1. Find debug macros.
2. Do not clear the working setup after seeing archive metadata.
3. Stop if replacement has not been applied.

It omits that the current revision and the revision of gradle-client-integration can change separately, and it does not state the latest return time for borrowed items. Therefore, it cannot be used by itself as a window check; but if these are the only three lines left in the setup, they can at least preserve the final output and the unreplaced entry point.

## Check in This Order Before Closeout

1. **Check the entry point first.** Write down the current entry point at the end of the window. If it is still the old value, preserve the old value and timestamp; do not immediately assume it is the cache, and do not immediately assume it is an old task. First check whether the command and revision fixed for this run are still in the same record.
2. **Then check the last output.** The corresponding exit code, gradle · Caller Integration, and tail log must come from the same execution. If all you have is the text "success," with no exit code or input, treat it as unconfirmed.
3. **Then handle the replacement.** When `Apply replacement` has appeared, still verify the artifact or entry-point state; success in the log is not evidence that the replacement has taken effect. If it has not appeared, stop in the unreplaced state; do not hide the original setup by rerunning.
4. **Return the borrowed items.** Before revoking temporary permissions and bypasses, confirm that the queue is not continuing to accept new work. While the queue is still receiving work, do not return the worker, environment, or proxy; stop new work first, then reclaim the temporary conditions.
5. **Write the rollback location.** If there is an old value, write the old value; if there is no old value, explicitly write "no known rollback location." Do not fabricate a rollback point just because the window has ended.

The goal of this order is not to make every integration test produce a record of the same length. Sometimes the current entry point can be confirmed quickly while the last output is missing; the output may also be complete while the entry point still targets the old cache. The checklist has only one common action in both cases: preserve the material already seen, stop at the first divergence without evidence, and do not fill in the subsequent judgment.

## Two Stopping Points

**The entry point is still old, but the output is visible.**

Keep the window-end timestamp, current entry point, and last output. Do not release the current revision and then ask why the entry point did not change. If the execution command differs from the two records, stop at the command difference; if the command is the same but the revisions differ, stop at the revision difference. DPTC-010 compare only the revisions of both gradle-client-integration entries, which is suitable for separating this layer; they do not replace confirmation of the cache or old task.

**The entry point has changed, but the output is incomplete.**

Do not clear the old setup just because the entry point has changed. Save whatever tail log can be obtained, and mark whether the exit code is missing, the integration-test identifier is missing, or both are missing. Then return to the old value from the rollback entry point; if the old value was not recorded, stop the rollback and do not write a guessed value into the entry point. An entry-point change and reviewable output are two separate things; the former cannot supply the latter.

**The two records differ.**

Place the two generation commands and their respective timestamps side by side first, and find the earliest difference. Stop further attribution as soon as the first divergence is found. Do not align subsequent logs line by line to prove which side is correct; this page currently lacks the context required for that comparison. DPTC-013 can take the person taking over back to the original comparison task.

## Rollback and Return

Rollback is not finished just by "switching the current entry point back to the old value." First confirm that no new work has entered the queue, then remove the temporary permissions and bypasses; otherwise, after returning to the old value, new requests may still continue executing under the temporary conditions. Borrowed items may be returned after the last output is saved, but not before the entry-point state is recorded.

- [ ] The exit code, integration-test identifier, and tail log from the last execution have been saved.
- [ ] The current entry point at the end of the window has been recorded; if the old cache or old task has not been ruled out, record it as unconfirmed.
- [ ] The artifact or state of `Apply replacement` has been checked; if it did not appear, remain stopped.
- [ ] After the queue no longer accepts new work, revoke the temporary permissions, bypasses, and actual borrowed items.
- [ ] During rollback, use only the recorded old value. If the old value is missing, do not perform a guess-based rollback.

The early wording treated "archive metadata exists" as a signal that cleanup could begin. That judgment is no longer reliable: the archive information may belong to the previous version, and the source field for the current result is still empty. The old wording is retained here to remind the person taking over why the working setup is often lost at closeout, not to treat archive metadata as completion evidence.

## Navigation Still in Use

To find the original checklist or attachment, start from `docs/adj-gradle/release/gradle-caller-integration-pre-window-close-checklist.md`. For version synchronization, final output, single-variable reruns, the old entry point, revisions on both sides, or record divergence, use DPTC-001, DPTC-003, DPTC-006, DPTC-008, DPTC-010, DPTC-013, and DPTC-015 respectively to return to the task context from that time.

DPTC-015 requires exporting the states before and after the failure first, once the current entry point is hit. Its relationship to this page is narrowly scoped: this page only reminds people to retain these states at closeout; it does not specify who analyzes them afterward or add runtime-side judgments.

This checklist is still retained using the terminology from the old window. If the entry point, rollback method, or borrowing conditions change later, write a separate record of the actual operation; do not insert the new process directly into these old stopping points.

# Quality Signal Hub Entry Migration Process

Migration records are kept in `docs/adj-license/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. This covers the old and current entry points for license-quality-signal, and does not fold similarly named side paths into the same batch.

The old entry point must not be deleted just because the current entry point appears in the directory. Each item must first have its actual callers identified; when a caller still enters through the old entry point, a directory update counts only as a navigation change, not as a completed migration. Notes that cannot be traced back must be kept as-is and marked as expired; this cannot be used to infer that callers have switched.

## Migration tracker

Keep one line for each old entry point: the old entry point name, the current entry-point location, callers still using it, the corresponding test failure sample, and that sample's place in the regression tiers. If a signal is unstable, also record which side it was attributed to at the time; do not put a one-off failure directly into the fixed regression set.

Each migration batch needs its own maintainer, schedule, and exit criteria. The maintainer is responsible for whether this batch can continue; that does not make the maintainer responsible for filling in the Quality Signal Hub's long-term meaning. Exit criteria must include at least: confirmed callers no longer enter through the old entry point, failure samples can still be archived under the current entry point, and unstable signals have not lost their attribution point because of the entry-point replacement.

## Execution order

1. List actual callers from the old entry point and leave the confirmation results in the migration tracker.
2. Determine the current entry-point location for each caller; if the location cannot be found, stop at this step and do not delete the old navigation first.
3. After replacing the entry point, review the failure records and regression tiers using the original test sample.
4. Only once confirmation is complete for all listed callers, mark the old entry point as an expired navigation item; the original records and dates remain available for lookup.

If the current entry point is already in the directory but the actual callers have not been confirmed, retain the old entry point. This distinguishes navigation cleanup from caller migration, so navigation cleanup does not prematurely overwrite caller migration.

## Rollback

If, after replacement, failure samples cannot be archived or unstable signals lose their original attribution point, restore the old entry point first and stop further replacements in this batch. After restoring it, record the affected callers and samples in the migration tracker; do not record this rollback as a completed migration. Whether to also roll back callers that have already been switched remains unresolved; first ensure that the old entry point is usable again.

New notes under the current entry point should add only replacement locations and confirmed callers. Record the old path, current entry point, and compatible callers separately, to avoid later cleanup misrecording a single navigation adjustment as completion of the entire migration batch.

# Release Freeze Handoff: Entry-Point Code Walkthrough

release-build shows up in several different places in the repository: build outputs, directory names, and old scripts. For the handoff, we need to find where the release freeze first gets used, not collect every file bearing that name. The starting point we've kept is still `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/bytesig.c`: a breadcrumb we were able to reconnect to the last time we traced back through call names.

The first draft made this path sound too much like "entering the release flow through this file." That conclusion was revised after review. The file's location only shows that nearby implementation code was previously read from there; whether to dig further depends on the call name provided by the public entry point of release-build, and whether the next hop can be established as a direct call. If that hop can't be found, return to the entry point and check. Don't use directory hierarchy to fill in the relationship.

```text
release-build public entry point
        |
        v
One direct caller
        |
        v
First actual consumer of the release freeze
        |
        v
Where the on-call handoff reads or interprets it
```

The diagram is not a component ownership map, and its arrows do not represent confirmed cross-directory links. It only sets the reading order for this pass: get the call name from the public entry point, choose one direct caller, then identify where the release freeze is first used among the subsequent objects. If the caller only formats data, joins paths, or converts names, reaching it does not yet mean we've entered freeze handling.

## Start with a narrow read of the entry point

There's no need to explain all the release parameters at the entry point or list every build variant. For this pass, keep only the call name that can be traced. Which direct caller picks it up after it leaves the entry point is the first relationship that needs to be established in code.

Once the direct caller is found, first look at what it passes the information to. It's easy to go off track here: an object appearing in the build process does not mean it determines whether the release is pinned, or that the on-call handoff gets state from it. Only keep a subsequent object on this trace-back path if it needs to use that information to read, pass on, or interpret release freeze information.

The "first actual consumer" is the point to stop looking for similar files; it does not mean you need to read through the rest of the release process. At this point, you should be able to state which call name led to that object and which part of the release freeze information it uses. If the on-call handoff simply jumps from here to another object, record that hop; if going further requires someone else to explain what the state means, leave the question here.

## Using the first error in the build log

The first-error build log is material for locating the problem. It answers whether this read-through is already blocked near the entry point or direct caller; it does not prove that a particular file is responsible for the release freeze. First look at the earliest failure location, then check whether it falls before or after the point being traced.

If the first error is near the entry point or direct caller, first work out whether this section of the path can still be followed; don't infer handoff state from later errors at this stage. If the first error is past the object being examined but the call chain still breaks before reaching the consumer, return to the last confirmed object and recheck where the input is passed. A file with the same name appearing in the log is only a prompt to recheck references, not grounds for adding that file directly to the diagram.

The full sequence of errors isn't retained on this page. Later errors in a compilation run often stem from the first one. For the handoff, the more useful detail is the location of the first failure: before the entry point, inside the direct caller, or after the consumer already identified. This keeps the next person reviewing it from mistaking noise from one compilation run for the source of release state.

## Two types of search results

The first type is files with the same name but no call edges. They may be close to release-build, or near the top of the search results. Just note them as breadcrumbs for now; unless a connecting call relationship turns up later, don't include them in the trace-back path. `bytesig.c` follows the same rule: it preserves previously visible code adjacency, but does not replace checking the calls at the entry point.

The second type is objects that consume build information but not freeze or handoff information. These objects are on release-adjacent paths, but they aren't the actual entry point we're looking for in this pass. To decide, check whether the object keeps the release freeze in effect, or lets the on-call handoff retrieve, pass on, or interpret that state; don't follow objects that only handle build data any further.

Once the consumer is confirmed, three short notes are enough: the call name used at the entry point, the release freeze information the consumer actually handles, and whether the handoff continues reading here or passes it to another object. Don't fold the same-named directories, old scripts, and cascading errors seen during the search into the path as well.

This review confirmed the trace-back order and changed the description of `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/bytesig.c` from a "release entry point" to a breadcrumb. The owners of the relevant locations still need to clarify the write side of the release freeze and whether the on-call handoff reads the same state.

title: NDK Baseline Window Deviation Postmortem

versions.body:
# NDK Baseline Window Discrepancy Review

NDK Within the baseline window, one visible result did not match the original plan. This was not classified on site as a single-point failure: the initial discovery, temporary recovery, and unresolved cause were three separate matters, and the record preserves that order.

The first artifact left behind was the application replacement timing trace. It shows that a replacement-related path appeared during observation, but the material available at the time was insufficient to determine whether the replacement happened too early, too late, or the trace captured only one segment of the actual process. The result from the window therefore cannot be treated as a clean baseline observation; that is closer to the scope the on-site team could confirm than saying "NDK baseline was already anomalous."

## Incident timeline

**Discovery.** The visible result expected by the original plan did not appear, or at least did not appear in the planned way. The team first reviewed the application replacement timing trace because it was the only runtime trace available at the time that could be reviewed directly alongside this discrepancy. The trace was still present; that does not mean the result had been explained. It only made replacement timing a direction for further investigation.

**Initial assessment.** At the time, someone focused on the NDK baseline window and thought the switch itself might have introduced the discrepancy. That framing was useful in the on-site response: it explained why the window result was initially not treated as a stable observation. But it was not supported by evidence that could independently distinguish the cause. The old record's wording was closer to "baseline discrepancy"; that working terminology is retained here, but it must not be read as a confirmed root cause.

**Search location.** The investigation followed NDK and the call name in the trace to the vicinity of `shell/src/main/cpp/bhook/third_party/lss/linux_syscall_support.h`. This location was the search entry point at the time, not a permanent ownership assignment for the issue. It is recorded because later investigators would re-enter through the same call name, not because the header file had been proven to change the window result.

**Temporary recovery.** The on-site team did not wait for the cause to be closed out before restoring the window's usability. Instead, it arranged to use a reversible old entry point so observation could continue. This action restored the arrangement's operability for that run. It did not fix a confirmed underlying defect, nor did it prove that the application replacement order had returned to the expected state.

**Follow-up note.** QA later separately recorded the actual impact, the coordinator, and whether the old entry point could be reverted. This was to prevent someone later seeing only the word "recovery" and conflating window recovery, result visibility, and cause confirmation into a single state. The recovery time should not be backfilled as the time when the root cause was already known.

## Impact that could be established at the time

The impact can be confirmed for this one window: the original plan could not provide the baseline observation as expected, and the related results need to be read in the context of the discrepancy. There is no evidence that all NDK builds were affected in the same way, nor that all runtime environments experienced an application replacement issue.

At the time, two situations could not yet be distinguished: one was that the replacement process itself differed from the expected order; the other was that the observation point did not cover the segment the plan expected to capture. The former would direct the investigation toward the replacement chain; the latter might simply mean that the trace's location or scope was unsuitable. Neither had been ruled out at the time.

The actual impact did not mean the runtime was unusable. When confidence in the window observation was lost, the old entry point still allowed the team to continue viewing the results; but "being able to continue viewing" did not mean the original observation conditions had been restored. This distinction was added to the record later.

## Retained old working hypothesis

> The discrepancy may be related to replacement timing in the NDK baseline window; use the old entry point to restore observation first; if the same sequence appears in the trace again, trace back via the call name.

This wording retains the rationale for the action at the time. It did not confirm replacement before context attach, nor did it designate ContextImpl or the component factory as the failure point. Replacement-related fragments in the trace can only indicate that these objects are worth comparing in the next observation; they do not allow a complete call sequence to be inferred from a single fragment.

Likewise, the window result's failure to match the plan does not automatically mean that the NDK baseline changed its behavior. The window was the context in which the discrepancy was found; the observation location, replacement order, and residual state from the old entry point could all have caused the visible result to diverge from the plan. At the time, the old entry point was a reversible recovery measure; this record did not reconfirm whether it should still be retained as a recovery option.

## Unresolved items

It remains unconfirmed whether the replacement fragment seen in the trace covered the actual location where the discrepancy occurred; nor has it been confirmed exactly where the window arrangement and the actual observation diverged. It is likewise unanswered whether the result seen after recovery merely became visible again while the application replacement itself retained its original order.

This record therefore leaves only a narrow historical judgment: the NDK baseline window once showed a result discrepancy, the on-site team used a reversible old entry point to restore the ability to continue observing, and the application replacement timing trace was retained as a lead for follow-up investigation. The term "baseline discrepancy" retained here is the wording used at the time; it should not be used as a conclusion about the current baseline state or as a conclusion attributing the issue to that header file.

# NDK Baseline Window FAQ

Q: What can the existing dex-runtime entry prove?

A: The initial review only covered `shell/src/main/cpp/dex/modifiers.h` and the names of nearby entries. The terms dex, runtime, Java, and native all appear here, indicating that someone at the time treated it as an inspection point where several processing stages meet; it is not a NDK baseline result, nor a complete record of the compilation process.

v1 turned "the entry is reachable" into "NDK baseline has passed". That judgment did not distinguish whether the entry existed, where compilation first failed, or whether the result could pass through the release pipeline. In the v2 review, the old answer was not deleted; one sentence was added stating that it cannot support a closure decision. The old wording remains because, when the window is brought up, people still use this sentence to treat the file entry as the baseline state.

A recheck of this entry can only verify whether the local relationship in dex/runtime still brings Java and native processing to the same place. If there are traces on both sides, that shows at most that the inspection point is not completely disconnected; it cannot replace rerunning the probes, nor can it be written up as meaning the candidate path is ready for release.

Q: Who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path?

A: This page does not confirm a fixed owner. The old draft assigned responsibility to the entry maintainer solely because the entry's location appeared closest to the candidate path; that was not authorization to withdraw it, and no corresponding withdrawal action can be verified. The later review still did not connect the candidate path, the actual withdrawal, and a specific owner in one record, so the old answer can now only be treated as a guess from that time.

The first-error compilation log is a question often added to this same window, but it was not filled in with an answer. Without the log, the location of the first error cannot be inferred from the entry name in `modifiers.h`, nor can the absence of a compilation problem be assumed just because the entry is visible. Leave this blank item as is; do not change "not found yet" to "there is no first error".

Q: Under what conditions can it be closed?

A: The latest field feedback states the closure condition: before closing, a non-implementer must rerun the affected Java and native probes and verify that the release pipeline has not lost the compatibility entry. The "and" in this sentence remains two actions that must both be completed, not an either/or.

The rerun by a non-implementer specifically targets the affected Java and native probes: the entry maintainer's own local result cannot replace this step. The release-pipeline check is whether the compatibility entry is still present; even if the probes have results, this check cannot be skipped. Conversely, the compatibility entry still being present does not mean both types of probes have been rerun.

This closure criterion does not infer who is responsible for withdrawing the candidate path. The withdrawal owner remains unconfirmed; the closure condition cannot be used to fill in a fixed owner. The first two versions did not include this explicit requirement; their old answers are retained to avoid misrepresenting the later closure approach as a judgment that had already been established at the time.
